segments.label: Weather and transport
segments.text: Know the processes connecting igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rock. Weathering breaks rock down. Erosion and transport move the pieces; deposition drops them.

segments.label: Burial and lithification
segments.text: Burial packs sediment together. Compaction and cementation turn loose grains into sedimentary rock.

segments.label: Metamorphism
segments.text: Heat and pressure change solid rock into metamorphic rock. Metamorphism does not require melting.

segments.label: Melt and crystallize
segments.text: Melting makes magma; cooling makes igneous rock. His key point: the rock cycle has many possible routes, not one fixed loop.

segments.label: Precambrian
segments.text: For the review, know the major divisions and their order. Precambrian comes first and includes most of Earth's history.

segments.label: Paleozoic
segments.text: Next is the Paleozoic, with diverse life in the seas and expanding onto land.

segments.label: Mesozoic
segments.text: Then comes the Mesozoic, the era that includes the dinosaurs.

segments.label: Cenozoic
segments.text: Cenozoic is youngest. Remember the four broad blocks; he did not ask you to memorize every period name.

segments.label: Build magnetic stripes
segments.text: Wegener had evidence for continental drift but lacked a convincing driving mechanism. At a mid-ocean ridge, new basalt records magnetic polarity as it cools. Older bands move outward and keep their original polarity. Matching stripes on both sides are evidence for seafloor spreading.

segments.label: Watch the plate age
segments.text: Away from the ridge, oceanic lithosphere becomes older, cooler, denser, and thicker. Keep the layers separate: mantle lithosphere thickens as it cools, sediment accumulates above, and crust stays roughly similar in thickness.

segments.label: Divergent
segments.text: Divergent plates move apart. New oceanic crust forms at the ridge, so this is a constructive boundary. Identify it from relative motion.

segments.label: Convergent
segments.text: Convergent plates move together. At a subduction zone, old oceanic lithosphere sinks and is recycled. That is the destructive boundary in the review.

segments.label: Transform
segments.text: Transform plates slide past: a conservative boundary. Crust is neither created nor consumed. On a map, count connected plate regions, then identify each boundary's motion.

segments.label: Earth layers
segments.text: Crust, mantle, and core describe composition. Lithosphere means rigid crust plus uppermost mantle. The asthenosphere below is weaker but mostly solid. The L A B separates those mechanical layers.

segments.label: Change thickness
segments.text: His wood-block analogy explains isostasy. At equal density, a thicker block rides higher and extends deeper. Thick continental crust helps explain high elevations.

segments.label: Change density
segments.text: At equal thickness, denser material sits lower. Compare thickness and density before predicting elevation. The floating blocks are an analogy, not a liquid mantle.

segments.label: First volcano
segments.text: Some volcanoes occur inside plates, away from plate boundaries. Rising hot mantle can partially melt at shallow depth and feed a hot spot.

segments.label: A chain grows
segments.text: The plate carries each volcano away from the active center. A new volcano grows over the same hot spot. The chain gets older away from activity.

segments.label: Trace plate motion
segments.text: Remember his examples: Hawaii in the ocean, and Yellowstone on a continent.

segments.label: Add heat
segments.text: Read the axes first. Temperature increases rightward; pressure increases downward. Heating moves the rock right. Crossing the solidus starts partial melting.

segments.label: Reduce pressure
segments.text: Now move upward: pressure decreases while temperature stays similar. That is decompression melting. Watch melt appear between grains that remain solid.

segments.label: Add water
segments.text: Water lowers the solidus. The same rock can start melting without becoming hotter. Know how all three changes appear on this graph.

segments.label: Crystal nuclei
segments.text: Texture records cooling history. Slow cooling gives crystals time to grow large. Faster cooling makes small crystals; very rapid cooling can make glass.

segments.label: Growth
segments.text: Watch the two-stage sample. Large crystals grow first during slow cooling. Faster cooling then produces the fine groundmass. That mixed texture is porphyritic.

segments.label: Final textures
segments.text: Explain the history, not just the texture name. He also emphasized pegmatites: water-rich melt helps atoms move efficiently and grow exceptionally large crystals.

segments.label: Bubble formation
segments.text: Vesicles are cavities made by gas bubbles in lava. As pressure falls, dissolved gas comes out of solution and bubbles begin to grow.

segments.label: Expansion
segments.text: The review compares pumice and scoria. Pumice commonly has many thin-walled cavities and can float. Scoria commonly has darker, thicker walls. Their compositions differ.

segments.label: Frozen vesicles
segments.text: Cooling preserves the bubbles as holes. These are vesicles, not crystals.

segments.label: Start cooling
segments.text: Read his chart in two steps: composition first, texture second. The composition groups are felsic, intermediate, mafic, and ultramafic.

segments.label: Compare crystal growth
segments.text: Granite and rhyolite can have similar composition. Slow cooling makes coarse granite; rapid cooling makes fine rhyolite. Likewise, compare diorite with andesite, and gabbro with basalt.

segments.label: Read the rock names
segments.text: Use the mineral bands too: quartz and potassium feldspar suggest felsic composition; olivine and pyroxene are characteristic of mafic and ultramafic rocks.

segments.label: Build a tetrahedron
segments.text: Oxygen and silicon dominate Earth's crust. One silicon surrounded by four oxygens makes a tetrahedron, the basic silicate unit. Learn both the structure and its name.

segments.label: Share corner oxygen
segments.text: Sharing corner oxygens links tetrahedra into chains, sheets, and frameworks. He also asked about non-silicates: name their group from the anion. Sulfide and sulfate differ because sulfate contains oxygen. Review ionic, covalent, metallic, and molecular bonds alongside these structures.

segments.label: High-temperature minerals
segments.text: Bowen's series describes crystallization order as magma cools. In the discontinuous branch, follow olivine, pyroxene, amphibole, then biotite. High-temperature minerals appear first.

segments.label: Continue cooling
segments.text: Plagioclase changes from calcium-rich toward sodium-rich. Potassium feldspar, muscovite, and quartz belong toward the low-temperature end.

segments.label: Partial melting
segments.text: Now reverse the reasoning. On heating, lower-melting components enter the liquid first. Partial melt is generally more silica-rich than its source, while solid minerals remain.

segments.label: Heat transfer
segments.text: Connect each melting mechanism to its setting. First, add heat: hot magma transfers energy into cooler surrounding rock, which may begin to melt.

segments.label: Decompression
segments.text: Second, reduce pressure. Mantle rising below ridges or hot spots can partially melt with little temperature change. This is decompression melting.

segments.label: Slab water
segments.text: Third, add water. Minerals in the descending slab release water into the mantle wedge. Water lowers the melting temperature. The whole slab does not simply melt.

segments.label: Magma rises
segments.text: His main connection is viscosity to volcano shape. Viscosity means resistance to flow. Watch how each eruption adds material to the slopes.

segments.label: Add deposits
segments.text: Low-viscosity basalt spreads far, building a broad shield such as Hawaii. More viscous magma and successive eruption deposits build a steeper composite volcano.

segments.label: Compare the shapes
segments.text: Mount Fuji and Mount Saint Helens were his composite examples. More silica generally increases viscosity. Explain why the material spreads out or builds up.

segments.label: Conduction
segments.text: Use the boiling-pot analogy. Conduction transfers heat through contact, such as through the pot and its handle. The solid material does not circulate.

segments.label: Convection
segments.text: Convection carries heat with moving material. Warm water rises, spreads, cools, and sinks. Follow a parcel around the cell, just as in his review.

segments.label: Radiation
segments.text: Radiation carries energy as electromagnetic waves. Then connect the mechanisms to geology: rising mantle carries heat, and hot magma can conduct heat into neighboring crust.

segments.label: Ocean–ocean
segments.text: At ocean-ocean convergence, one plate descends, commonly the older, colder, denser one. Use density and temperature to explain which plate sinks.

segments.label: Ocean–continent
segments.text: At ocean-continent convergence, dense oceanic lithosphere subducts beneath more buoyant continental crust. Identify the plate types before naming the process.

segments.label: Continent–continent
segments.text: Two continents resist deep subduction. Collision shortens and thickens their crust, building mountains. Remember India, Asia, and the Himalaya as the review example.
